title: Isandro and the Interior
premise: After her mother's funeral, Tamsin Nystrom returns to the family house on the edge of the Interior district, a condemned neighborhood slated for demolition, to catalog her mother's belongings and her silences. A stranger at the funeral calls the family by their old name—Nystrom was an alias—and Tamsin begins pulling at a thread that reveals her mother sheltered fugitives from an unjust conviction decades ago. As demolition day approaches and developers press to raze the house with its hidden records inside, Tamsin must decide whether to expose the truth, which would clear one man's name but indict another who is now a beloved civic figure. In the end she translates her mother's final coded letter, delivers it publicly on the eve of demolition, and lets the house fall while carrying its history forward as her own name.
about_author: Juniper Coldharbour is the pen name of a former archivist who spent twelve years cataloging unclaimed estates in northern port cities. Their fiction explores inheritance, silence, and the small justices people arrange outside official systems.

chapters.title: The Tenant's Key
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Days after the funeral, she moves through her childhood house like a renter, cataloging objects for an estate sale she keeps postponing. The emotional beat is numb displacement—grief experienced as bureaucracy.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: At the memorial reception, an elderly stranger grips Tamsin's arm and says, 'You're one of the Vaskr children.' Tamsin has never heard the name. POV shifts briefly to the stranger, Edda, watching Tamsin leave. Beat: first crack in the inherited silence.

chapters.title: Inventory of Absences
chapters.summary: Tamsin catalogs rooms and finds gaps: no photos before 1989, a locked trunk, her mother's habit of burning papers each autumn. She interviews the neighbor Mr. Oyelaran, who deflects carefully. Beat: suspicion replacing grief.

chapters.title: The Interior District
chapters.summary: Tamsin walks the condemned neighborhood her mother refused to leave, meeting residents fighting the demolition order. She learns her mother paid rents quietly for families facing eviction. Beat: her mother becomes a stranger with a public shadow.

chapters.title: Edda's Ledger
chapters.summary: Edda visits with a battered ledger of names, dates, and sums—the Vaskr family's underground network that hid witnesses after a wrongful conviction in the mill trials. Beat: vertigo of discovering a second family history.

chapters.title: The Trunk
chapters.summary: Tamsin pries open the locked trunk: false passports, a child's drawing signed with her birth name, and one sealed letter written in a private cipher her mother invented for them as a game. Beat: tenderness weaponized into secrecy.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: The city posts final demolition orders; the house has ninety days. Developer representative Callum Reyes offers Tamsin a generous buyout and mentions, too casually, that 'records' in the district should stay buried. Beat: pressure arrives wearing a smile.

chapters.title: The Man Who Stayed
chapters.summary: POV chapter of Jonas Pell, the convicted man now a celebrated philanthropist whose exoneration case died with the witnesses. He receives an anonymous note about the funeral. Beat: the past acquiring a heartbeat.

chapters.title: Cipher Lessons
chapters.summary: Tamsin works the cipher using childhood games as the key, decoding fragments: 'the third witness,' 'what Halvard took,' 'do not trust the ledger alone.' Beat: intimacy with the dead mother through puzzle-solving.

chapters.title: Halvard
chapters.summary: Edda reveals Halvard Vaskr—Tamsin's uncle—who informed on the network to save himself and rose into the establishment he once betrayed. Beat: the family myth inverts; shame enters the inheritance.

chapters.title: Callum's Second Offer
chapters.summary: Reyes raises the buyout and hints the firm represents interests connected to Pell's foundation. Tamsin realizes the demolition isn't just urban renewal—it's erasure. Beat: righteous anger kindling.

chapters.title: The Third Witness
chapters.summary: Decoded pages identify a third witness still alive: Ruth Amankwah, living under a protected identity two towns over. Tamsin travels to find her. Beat: hope with a time limit.

chapters.title: Ruth
chapters.summary: Ruth refuses at first—she built a life on burial—but confirms the mill fire was arson ordered by the mill owners, and that Halvard sold out the witnesses. Beat: testimony as burden passed hand to hand.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Back home, Tamsin finds the physical evidence her mother preserved: documents hidden in the walls, indexed in the ledger. The house itself is the archive. Beat: the building transforms from prison to sanctuary.

chapters.title: Jonas Comes Calling
chapters.summary: Pell arrives at the house, asking—not demanding—for the evidence, offering money and protection. Tamsin reads his desperation and his decency and cannot tell which is real. Beat: moral ambiguity at full strength.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: The final cipher passage resists translation; Tamsin realizes the key is a sentence her mother said only once, at the hospital: 'Some names you keep so other names can live.' Beat: grief resolving into understanding.

chapters.title: Betrayal in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Edda confesses she copied the ledger years ago and sold a page to Pell's rivals to fund the residents' legal fight—an act that endangered everyone. Trust fractures within the resistance. Beat: justice outside the law shows its costs.

chapters.title: Ninety Becomes Nine
chapters.summary: The demolition date moves up after a fire scare—engineered, Tamsin suspects, by Reyes's clients. The group must act in days, not months. Beat: rising panic, compressed stakes.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Climax part one: at a public hearing, Tamsin reads the decoded letter aloud, naming Halvard, the mill owners, and her mother's network, with Ruth present as living witness. Beat: exposure as both liberation and wound.

chapters.title: Demolition Day
chapters.summary: Climax part two: as machines arrive, Tamsin retrieves the last documents, refuses Reyes's final check, and stands with neighbors as the house falls. Pell watches from across the street, unnamed and undone. Beat: destruction as witness-bearing.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Filed Under T.N.
chapters.summary: Investigations reopen; Halvard's reputation cracks; Pell withdraws from public life pending review. Tamsin feels neither triumphant nor clean. Beat: the hangover of truth-telling.

chapters.title: Owner of Her Own Name
chapters.summary: Epilogue: Tamsin signs the estate papers, legally reclaiming Vaskr alongside Nystrom, and takes a job archiving the Interior district's oral histories before they scatter. Beat: belonging chosen rather than inherited.
